items.title: Fix SSI spousal deeming for in-kind support and for aged, blind or disabled spouses who are not eligible
items.body:
## What

Two federal SSI defects in couple and spousal-deeming cases. Both came up while answering the review of PR 10165 (Oklahoma SSP).

### 1. Spousal deeming uses the $20 general exclusion twice when the eligible spouse has in-kind support

`ssi_income_deemed_from_ineligible_spouse` measures the deemed amount as couple countable income minus the eligible spouse's countable income alone. Neither figure includes in-kind support and maintenance (ISM). `ssi_countable_income` then adds the ISM to the eligible spouse's own countable income, which takes its own $20 exclusion.

The deeming steps in 20 CFR 416.1163 combine the eligible spouse's income with the ineligible spouse's deemed income and apply the $20 exclusion once.

Probe (2026-01, Oklahoma):
- Household: aged claimant who receives outside shelter support (PMV 258.50) and a 62-year-old spouse with $700 a month of Social Security.
- Model: countable income is 918.50 (238.50 + 680), so SSI is 572.50.
- One exclusion: 258.50 + 700 − 20 = 938.50, so SSI would be 552.50.

### 2. The couple classification ignores whether the aged, blind or disabled spouse is eligible

`ssi_claim_is_joint`, `is_ssi_eligible_spouse` and `is_ssi_ineligible_spouse` look only at aged, blind or disabled status. A spouse who doesn't take up SSI, or is barred for immigration status, still gets a couple computation. 20 CFR 416.1160(d) and 416.1801(c) define an ineligible spouse as one who is not eligible for SSI, and deeming then applies (POMS SI 00501.154).

Probe (2026-01):
- Household: aged claimant with $500 a month of Social Security, and an aged spouse with $300 a month who doesn't take up SSI.
- Model: a couple computation, (500 + 300 − 20) / 2 = 390, so the claimant's SSI is 745.50 − 390 = 355.50.
- Under deeming: the spouse's $300 is at most the $497 allocation, so nothing is deemed and SSI would be 994 − 480 = 514.

items.title: SSI: deemed benefit is capped at the individual rate instead of the no-deeming amount, and couples are identified by tax roles
items.body:
Two SSI gaps, found while registering a population analysis in PolicyEngine/microcosm-dynamics and reproduced on `main` at `bee8954716` (2.39.1) with invented households (2026: individual rate $994, couple rate $1,491, resource limits $2,000 and $3,000).

## 1. Spousal deeming caps the benefit at the individual rate, not at the benefit without deeming

`ssi_if_takes_up` caps SSI at the individual Federal benefit rate whenever spousal income deeming applies. 20 CFR 416.1163(e)(2) says:

> Your SSI benefit under the deeming rules cannot be higher than it would be if deeming did not apply. Therefore, your benefit is the lesser of the amount computed under the rules in paragraph (d)(2) of this section or the amount remaining after we subtract only your own countable income from an individual's Federal benefit rate.

The cap is the claimant's no-deeming benefit, which is below the individual rate whenever the claimant has countable income of their own.

Florida couple: claimant aged 70 with Social Security of $743 a month and $1,500 in the bank; spouse aged 64 with Social Security of $100 and wages of $400 a month.

| | main | 416.1163 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Spouse income $500 > $497, so deeming applies | $500.50 a month ($1,491 − $990.50) | $271 a month (lesser of $500.50 and $994 − $723) |
| Same couple with Social Security cut to $579 and $78 (spouse income $478, no deeming) | $435 a month | $435 a month |

On `main`, the cut lowers the couple's income and also lowers annual SSI, from $6,006 to $5,220. Under the regulation SSI rises from $3,252 to $5,220.

Related: 416.1163(f)(5) deems no spousal income while the $30 medical facility rate applies, but `main` subtracts deemed income from the $30.

## 2. SSI couples are identified by tax-unit roles

`ssi_claim_is_joint` requires both spouses to be the head or spouse of their tax unit. When roles are not supplied, PE-US gives those roles to the two oldest adults of the tax unit. The ineligible spouse used for income deeming (`is_ssi_ineligible_spouse`) has the same dependency. Under 20 CFR 416.1801(c), an eligible spouse is someone eligible for SSI who is the spouse of another person eligible for SSI and lives in the same household. Under 416.1160(d), an ineligible spouse is "someone who lives with you as your husband or wife and is not eligible for SSI benefits". Neither definition refers to tax roles.

- An aged couple aged 70 and 68 (Social Security $700 and $600), sharing a tax unit with a 90-year-old: the wife is a tax dependent, so `main` computes two individuals at $314 and $414 a month. Under 416.1802(b) and 416.412 they are a couple: $1,491 − $1,280 = $211, or $105.50 each.
- The same structure with a non-aged husband who is a tax dependent: the husband's $2,000 a month of wages is not deemed to the claimant, so `main` pays $414 a month. Under 416.1163 the claimant's countable income exceeds the couple rate, so the payment is $0.
- A citizen aged 70 married to an undocumented aged 68-year-old is a joint claim on `main`, because the joint test reads only aged/blind/disabled status. Under 416.1801(c) the spouse is not eligible for SSI, so their income should be deemed.

Resource deeming (416.1202, 416.1205) was missing in the 2.18.0 release where this was first seen. #10040 added it, so that part already holds on `main`: an ineligible spouse's $3,500 now fails the $3,000 couple limit. #10040 listed the joint-claim and income-deeming role dependency as a known limitation.

Pinned regulation copies (Cornell LII, with SHA-256 values) and the reviewer scripts are in the microcosm-dynamics evidence folder for the depletion-cut registration (`pe-us-depletion-cut-population-20261001/sources/`).

items.title: State supplements under SSI spousal deeming should compare individual and couple state computations (POMS SI 01320.430)
items.body:
Found during the independent review of #10141. This was already on `main`; #10141 doesn't change it.

Several federally administered state supplements reduce the supplement by the federal SSI shortfall, `max(0, -uncapped_ssi)`:
- `policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/de/dhss/ssp/de_ssp.py`
- `policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/dc/dhcf/ossp/dc_ossp.py`
- `policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/hi/dhs/oss/hi_oss.py`
- `policyengine_us/variables/gov/states/ma/dta/ssp/ma_state_supplement.py`

POMS SI 01320.430 D.1–D.3 covers an eligible individual living with an ineligible spouse when deeming applies. It says the state supplement is computed separately on an individual basis and on a couple basis, and the state then applies its own lesser-of comparison. 20 CFR 416.1163(d)(2)(iii) points to 416.2025(b).

Reviewer's example for Delaware (2026), not yet re-run: the claimant has no income, and the ineligible spouse has a pension of $1,531 a month. Combined countable income is $1,511, which leaves a federal shortfall of $20. The model pays $120. The state comparison gives min(140, 448 − 20) = $140.

Tasks:
- Check the example against Delaware's parameters.
- Implement both bases and the comparison for each state.
- Add YAML cases with values hand-computed from POMS and each state's payment levels.

items.title: Orange County General Relief: audit findings vs. GR Regulations Manual and Handbook
items.body:
## Summary

The Orange County General Relief implementation (`ca_oc_general_relief`, under `policyengine_us/{variables,parameters}/gov/local/ca/oc/general_relief/`) was compared against Orange County's official sources:

- **GR Regulations Manual** — the legal basis (W&I Code §§17000–17410, county-delegated); sections published at [ssa.ocgov.com](https://www.ssa.ocgov.com/page/general-relief-regulations).
- **GR Handbook** — the caseworker procedures manual (obtained via a public-records request). The Handbook matters here because it contains the actual **MAP** and **component-value** figures that the Regulations Manual omits.

The model is **faithful for the dominant case** — a single childless adult with cash income. The items below are discrepancies or gaps found against the primary-source text. Each was verified against the actual Manual/Handbook language. **Filing for a more careful review later — not yet actioned.**

## Verified faithful (no change expected)

- Benefit = MAP − net countable income, floored at 0 (Manual §80.2.d).
- MAP size-1 = **$355**, effective 10/1/2016 — corroborated by the Handbook §80.3 grant-computation example.
- Earned-income **20% standard deduction**; deductions for health-insurance premiums and verified court-ordered child/spousal support (§70.2.o/p).
- Energy Assistance and CalFresh allotments correctly excluded from counted income (§70.2.d, §70.3.a).
- Personal-property limit **$1,000**; vehicle exclusion **$4,650** (§60.2.a, §60.4.c).
- Adult age ≥ 18; children excluded from the MAP (§10.6.v, §80.3.d(1)).
- Immigration list (CITIZEN, LPR, withholding-of-deportation) matches the two eligible non-citizen categories named in §40.1.

## Discrepancies (verified against primary sources)

| Finding | Severity | Source | Code |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Shared-housing reduction is a flat 15%, but the regulation is tiered 15% / 20% / 25%** for sharing with 1 / 2 / 3+ others. The model keys off the boolean `is_shared_living` and never counts co-residents, so it overpays units sharing with 2+ people. (Structural — a fix needs household size minus EU size.) | Medium | Manual §80.3.a(3) (p.45) | `payment/shared_housing_reduction.yaml`, `payment/ca_oc_general_relief_max_aid_payment.py` |
| **Outdated comment + unmodeled component-value deductions.** `ca_oc_general_relief.py` says component-value deductions aren't modeled "because Orange County does not publish the component-value dollar amounts" — but the Handbook §80.3 publishes the percentages (**Housing/Utilities 65%, Food 28%, Transportation 5%, Clothing 2%**), so the dollar values are derivable as %×MAP. The Housing/Utility Excess Component Value and the free-component deductions are genuinely unmodeled (applying them needs household shelter-cost inputs PolicyEngine generally lacks). At minimum the comment should be corrected. | Medium | Handbook §80.3 (Grant Computation) | `ca_oc_general_relief.py` |
| **$50 liquid-resource rule unmodeled.** Cash/liquid resources over $50 should reduce the initial-month MAP (§60.2.a) and count as income (§70.2.g); the model uses cash only for the $1,000 property test. The integration-test comment "cash … no longer counted as income" appears to be a mistaken rationale (it conflates active §70.2.g with the deleted §70.2.e). | Medium | Manual §60.2.a (p.35), §70.2.g (p.39) | `resources/ca_oc_general_relief_countable_property.py`, `income/ca_oc_general_relief_countable_income_person.py` |
| **MAP table provenance / currency.** The table is sourced from a 2015 OC HCA "DUI Program Standards" document and a 2017 Continuum-of-Care application — not the official "GR MAP Tables" (which appear only as an external hyperlink in the Handbook, not in any obtained record). Sizes 2–10 are assumed (flat +$5, self-documented in the YAML) and all values are frozen at 2016. Only size-1 is independently documented. Recommend obtaining the live GR MAP Tables to verify multi-person amounts and the current-year value. | Medium | Handbook §80.3 (external link) | `payment/max_aid_payment.yaml` |
| **GR/CalWORKs split-EU MAP-differencing never reached.** CalWORKs/CAPI receipt is read at the SPM-unit level and flags every member, so a mixed unit (e.g. a child-only CalWORKs case plus a GR-needing adult) is marked categorically ineligible and gets $0, whereas §80.3.a(1) would pay MAP(all members) − MAP(CalWORKs members). | Medium | Manual §20.4.b, §80.3.a(1) (p.12/45) | `eligibility/ca_oc_general_relief_receives_other_cash_assistance.py`, `eligibility/ca_oc_general_relief_eligible_person_count.py` |
| **Fully-employed categorical bar not applied.** §30.9 makes a fully-employed adult categorically ineligible; the model applies only the income test, and the 20% disregard lets someone grossing ≈ the grant still pass and collect ~20% of MAP. | Medium | Manual §30.9.a-b | `eligibility/ca_oc_general_relief_income_eligible.py` |
| **Excluded non-PA member's income over-counted.** For an excluded member who isn't on other cash aid (e.g. an ineligible-noncitizen earner), only income above that member's own MAP-needs should be deemed to the aided unit (§70.3.a); the model counts their full income. | Medium | Manual §70.3.a | `income/ca_oc_general_relief_countable_income_person.py` |
| **Shared-housing exemption proxy mismatch.** The regulation exempts those in Housing Support Programs / homeless shelters / transitional housing; the model proxies this with `receives_housing_assistance` (HUD Section 8 / public housing), a different concept. | Low | Manual §80.3.a(3) | `payment/ca_oc_general_relief_max_aid_payment.py` |
| **Real-property limit not modeled** ($5,000 primary residence; secondary real property within the $1,000 cap) — only cash + vehicle are checked. Documented as a partner-data limitation. | Low | Manual §50.2 (p.32) | `resources/ca_oc_general_relief_countable_property.py` |

## Known framework limitations (listed for completeness; generally not fixable in a static model)

90-day/12-month employable time limit (§30.7.c); employability classification and mandatory GRWP/CFET participation (§30.6/30.7); incarcerated/institutionalized bar (§30.10); mandatory SSI/SSP application as a condition of aid (§30.4); cross-program sanction / lump-sum / property-disposal bars (§10.3); 15-day durational county residence (§40.2); sponsor income/resource deeming (§90.2); responsible-relative / community-property deeming (§90.1); period of ineligibility for lump sums (§70.2.i/r); 2-year disqualifying property transfers (§50.8/60.5); probation-violator / fleeing-felon bars (§30.11/30.12); roomer/boarder and educational-grant income refinements (§70.2.c/m/n).

## Notes

- Findings were cross-checked against the actual Manual/Handbook text; page numbers refer to the compiled PDFs.
- The single-adult cash case — by far the largest share of the GR caseload — is modeled correctly; the discrepancies mostly affect shared-housing units, mixed-aid households, and recipients with in-kind support or below-component-value shelter costs.

---
🤖 Issue drafted with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) from an audit of the implementation against Orange County's GR Regulations Manual and GR Handbook.

items.title: Missouri SAB: drop SSI-style $20 exclusion, spousal deeming, and student exclusion; key couple resource test on the marital unit; require a remainder
items.body:
Reported by MyFriendBen during their Missouri Supplemental Aid to the Blind (SAB) review. Verified against the MO DSS SAB manual, MHABD Appendix K (07/2026), and 13 CSR 40-2.120. Variables reviewed: `mo_sab_countable_income`, `mo_ssp_resource_eligible`, `mo_ssp_eligible`.

## 1. Parameters one update behind

Appendix K (07/2026) lists a $949 maximum payment and resource limits of $6,220.50 (individual) and $12,441.00 (couple), effective 2026-07-01. The model has $917, $6,068.80, and $12,137.55. The $1,073 consolidated standard already matches.

- `gov/states/mo/dss/ssp/sab/maximum_payment.yaml`
- `gov/states/mo/dss/ssp/eligibility/resource_limit/sab/{individual,couple}.yaml`

## 2. No $20 general exclusion in SAB

`mo_sab_countable_income` runs income through `_apply_ssi_exclusions`, which takes the SSI $20 general exclusion off unearned income. Missouri counts all of the applicant's income unless excluded ([13 CSR 40-2.120(2)(B)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/missouri/13-CSR-40-2-120)). The SAB exclusion list ([§ 0410.015.15](https://dssmanuals.mo.gov/supplemental-aid-to-the-blind/0410-000-00/0410-015-00/0410-015-15/)) has no general disregard, and the earned exemptions are enumerated in [§ 0410.015.05.20](https://dssmanuals.mo.gov/supplemental-aid-to-the-blind/0410-000-00/0410-015-00/0410-015-05/0410-015-05-20/): the first $85 plus half the remainder, federal and state income tax, Social Security tax, and a 10% personal standard (or higher actual work expenses). The only $20 disregard in 13 CSR 40-2 belongs to the MHABD Medicaid rule.

Example: $1,073/month pension income gives $1,053 countable and eligible in the model; Missouri counts $1,073.

## 3. No spousal deeming in SAB

`mo_sab_countable_income` adds `ssi_income_deemed_from_ineligible_spouse`. Appendix K page 5: "SAB income test is calculated individually, regardless of marital status." 13 CSR 40-2.120(2)(B): another household member's income is considered only in the amount actually made available. Drop the deemed amount.

Example: blind applicant with $500/month pension and a non-blind spouse earning $1,300/month gets $480 own plus $617.50 deemed and is ineligible in the model.

## 4. No SSI student earned-income exclusion in SAB

`mo_sab_countable_income` subtracts `ssi_blind_or_disabled_working_student_exclusion` from earnings. § 0410.015.05.20 says the Standard Earned Income Exemption Table "contains all earned income exemptions for the SAB claimant"; the SSI student exclusion is not among them.

## 5. Couple resource test keyed on the SPM unit, not the claimant's marital unit

`mo_ssp_resource_eligible` reads `spm_unit_is_married`, which is true when any tax unit in the SPM unit has a spouse. `is_tax_unit_spouse` ranks the oldest non-head adult as the spouse, so an unmarried 22-year-old in a parent's tax unit is treated as married and tested against the couple limit on the parents' combined resources. Missouri applies the couple limit only when the claimant is married and living with the spouse ([§ 1035.005.00](https://dssmanuals.mo.gov/december-1973-eligibility-requirements/1035-000-00/1035-005-00/)); separated spouses each use the individual limit.

Fix: `married = person.marital_unit.nb_persons() == 2`, the same pattern as #9379. The resource sum already uses `marital_unit.sum`. Applies to both the SAB and SNC branches.

## 6. SAB need test requires a remainder

`mo_ssp_eligible` uses `countable_income <= consolidated_standard`. [§ 0410.020.00](https://dssmanuals.mo.gov/supplemental-aid-to-the-blind/0410-000-00/0410-020-00/): "If there is a remainder, the claimant meets the SAB need determination. If there is no remainder, the claimant is ineligible for SAB based on need." Use `<`.

## Tests

- Kate's cases above, plus a $1,073 pension case that is ineligible after item 2 and item 6 together.
- Resource: a 22-year-old with $8,000 in their own marital unit inside a parent's tax unit (ineligible against $6,220.50), and the same pair declared as a marital unit (eligible under $12,441.00).

items.title: Spousal relationships
items.body:
Calculating SSI requires knowing spousal relationships. For example, if two adults in the household are SSI-eligible, they are treated different depending on if they're married. How can we denote this?

One idea: Assign them to the same family, and add an `is_married` flag. Technically this aligns with the Census's [subfamily](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/cps/technical-documentation/subject-definitions.html#subfamily) concept:
>A subfamily is a married couple with or without children, or a single parent with one or more own never-married children under 18 years old.

items.title: Marital units must be explicitly defined in test cases for SSI calculations to work correctly
items.body:
## Problem Description

When writing SSI test cases, marital units must be explicitly defined in the YAML test input. Without explicit marital unit definitions, SSI calculations produce incorrect results.

## Current Behavior

Test cases must include explicit marital unit definitions like:
```yaml
marital_units:
  marital_unit:
    members: [adult1, adult2]
```

Without this, SSI calculations that depend on marital units (like `ssi_claim_is_joint`) fail or return incorrect values.

## Expected Behavior

Marital units should be automatically inferred based on:
- Tax unit relationships (head and spouse)
- Family relationships  
- Marriage status indicators

This would align with how other entities work and reduce boilerplate in test cases.

## Affected SSI Variables

Variables that depend on marital units include:
- `ssi_claim_is_joint` - uses `person.marital_unit.sum()`
- `ssi_marital_earned_income`
- `ssi_marital_unearned_income` 
- `ssi_marital_both_eligible`
- Spousal deeming calculations (`ssi_earned_income_deemed_from_ineligible_spouse`, etc.)

## Impact

This affects:
1. Test writing - requires extra boilerplate
2. Web app functionality - may not correctly handle SSI for married couples
3. Microsimulation accuracy - SSI benefits for couples may be incorrectly calculated

## Proposed Solution

Implement automatic marital unit inference similar to how tax units are handled, possibly based on:
- `is_tax_unit_spouse` relationship
- Marriage status indicators
- Cohabitation patterns in households

## Related Code Locations

- Entity definition: `policyengine_us/entities.py` lines 75-91
- SSI joint claim: `policyengine_us/variables/gov/ssa/ssi/ssi_claim_is_joint.py`
- Test examples: `policyengine_us/tests/policy/baseline/gov/ssa/ssi/integration_tests.yaml`

items.title: Bug: MSP married couple income test uses individual income against couple FPL threshold (doubles effective household limit)
items.body:
## Summary

`msp_countable_income` uses each spouse's individual income when determining MSP eligibility for married couples, but it compares that individual income against the couple FPL threshold. This effectively doubles the household's income limit for married couples.

## Root cause

`msp_countable_income` (`:policyengine_us/variables/gov/hhs/medicare/savings_programs/income/msp_countable_income.py`) calls `_apply_ssi_exclusions` on each person's individual `ssi_earned_income` / `ssi_unearned_income`. MSP is statutorily required to use SSI income methodology (42 U.S.C. 1396d(p)(1)(B)), which for couples means aggregating both spouses' income first — as SSI's own `ssi_countable_income` does via `ssi_marital_earned_income` / `ssi_marital_unearned_income`.

There are two interrelated problems:

**1. Income is not aggregated for married couples**

SSI's `ssi_countable_income` uses `ssi_marital_earned_income` and `ssi_marital_unearned_income`, which return the couple's combined income attributed to each spouse when both are eligible. `msp_countable_income` skips this aggregation and uses individual income only.

**2. The $20 general income exclusion is applied twice**

Because `_apply_ssi_exclusions` is called per-person, a married couple each receives the $20/month general exclusion — $40/month total. Under SSI couple rules, the $20 exclusion is applied once to the couple's combined income.

## Effect

Each spouse's individual countable income (based only on their own income, with their own $20 exclusion) is independently compared against the full couple FPL threshold in `is_qmb_eligible`, `is_slmb_eligible`, and `is_qi_eligible`. The household's effective income limit is approximately 2× the couple FPL.

## Concrete example

2024 couple QMB threshold: $20,440/year = $1,703/month (100% FPL)

| | Spouse A | Spouse B |
|---|---|---|
| Unearned income | $15,000/yr | $15,000/yr |
| Countable (current, per-person) | $1,247/mo | $1,247/mo |
| Compared against | $1,703/mo | $1,703/mo |
| **Current result** | **QMB eligible** ✗ | **QMB eligible** ✗ |

Correct behavior: combined income = $30,000/yr → $2,480/mo after one $20 exclusion → exceeds $1,703 couple threshold → **neither eligible**.

## Why existing tests don't catch this

The integration test (`integration.yaml`) uses $9,000/yr unearned income per spouse → ~$730/mo countable each. Even combined (~$1,480/mo) this is below the couple QMB threshold (~$1,703/mo), so the test passes regardless. The bug only manifests when combined income exceeds the couple threshold while each individual income stays below it.

## Correct fix

`msp_countable_income` should:
1. Aggregate both spouses' income when both are Medicare-eligible (analogous to `ssi_marital_both_eligible` but conditioned on Medicare eligibility)
2. Apply `_apply_ssi_exclusions` once to the combined amount
3. **Not** divide by 2 (unlike `ssi_countable_income`) — MSP compares against the couple FPL, not a per-person benefit rate

Both spouses would then share the same `msp_countable_income` value (the couple's combined countable income), and both independently compare against the couple FPL in the eligibility variables.

The secondary case — one spouse Medicare-eligible, one not — would also need handling, mirroring SSI's spousal deeming logic.

## Files affected

- `policyengine_us/variables/gov/hhs/medicare/savings_programs/income/msp_countable_income.py`
- `policyengine_us/variables/gov/hhs/medicare/savings_programs/category/is_qmb_eligible.py`
- `policyengine_us/variables/gov/hhs/medicare/savings_programs/category/is_slmb_eligible.py`
- `policyengine_us/variables/gov/hhs/medicare/savings_programs/category/is_qi_eligible.py`
- `policyengine_us/tests/policy/baseline/gov/hhs/medicare/savings_programs/integration.yaml` (needs a test case that exposes the bug)

items.title: SSI spousal deeming uses wrong FBR: couples lose benefit when deeming applies
items.body:
# Critical Bug: SSI Spousal Deeming Uses Individual FBR Instead of Couple FBR

## Executive Summary

There is a **critical bug** in the SSI spousal deeming implementation. When spousal deeming applies (ineligible spouse's gross income > $483/month), the code incorrectly uses the **individual FBR** ($967/month) instead of the **couple FBR** ($1,450/month) as required by 20 CFR §416.1163.

**This causes couples to receive $483/month ($5,796/year) LESS than they should when deeming applies.**

---

## How SSI Spousal Deeming Should Work

According to 20 CFR §416.1163 and SSA POMS SI 01320.400, there are three scenarios for married couples:

### Scenario A: Both Spouses Eligible
- **Condition:** Both are aged/blind/disabled
- **FBR Used:** Couple rate ($1,450/month)
- **Calculation:** Combine incomes, apply exclusions, subtract from couple FBR, divide by 2
- **Status:** ✅ Working correctly

### Scenario B: One Eligible, No Deeming
- **Condition:** One aged/blind/disabled, ineligible spouse's gross income ≤ $483/month
- **FBR Used:** Individual rate ($967/month)
- **Calculation:** Only eligible spouse's income counted
- **Status:** ✅ Working correctly

### Scenario C: One Eligible, Deeming Applies
- **Condition:** One aged/blind/disabled, ineligible spouse's gross income > $483/month
- **FBR Used:** **Couple rate ($1,450/month)**
- **Calculation:** Combine incomes, apply exclusions, subtract from couple FBR, cap at individual FBR
- **Status:** ❌ **BROKEN** - Uses individual rate instead of couple rate

---

## The Bug

### Current (Broken) Code in `ssi_amount_if_eligible.py`

```python
head_or_spouse_amount = where(
    person("ssi_claim_is_joint", period),  # Only TRUE when BOTH eligible
    p.couple / 2,
    p.individual,  # ❌ WRONG for deeming scenarios
)
```

### What's Wrong

The variable `ssi_claim_is_joint` only returns `True` when **both spouses are aged/blind/disabled**.

When only one spouse is eligible:
- `ssi_claim_is_joint` = `False`
- Code uses `p.individual` ($967)
- This is correct for Scenario B (no deeming)
- **But wrong for Scenario C (deeming applies)** - should use `p.couple` ($1,450)

The code fails to distinguish between Scenario B and Scenario C, always using the individual rate for both.

---

## Understanding the Deeming Threshold

**Key regulatory point:** The $483 threshold compares the spouse's **GROSS income** (after child allocations only), **NOT** the countable income after $20/$65 exclusions.

### Deeming Decision Process:
1. Get ineligible spouse's gross income
2. Subtract child allocations (if any)
3. **Compare to $483 threshold**
   - If ≤ $483: No deeming (use individual FBR)
   - If > $483: Deeming applies (use couple FBR)
4. If deeming applies, **then** apply $20/$65 exclusions to combined income
5. Calculate benefit and cap at individual FBR

---

## Real-World Impact Examples

### Example 1: Spouse Earns $1,100/month

**Family:**
- Woman: Healthy, earns $1,100/month gross
- Man: Disabled, $0 income
- No children

**Does deeming apply?**
- Woman's gross: $1,100 > $483 → **YES**

**Combined countable:**
- Combined: $1,100/month
- Exclusions: $1,100 - $20 - $65 = $1,015
- Half: $1,015 / 2 = $507.50/month

**Before PR (WRONG):**
- Uses individual FBR: $967/month
- SSI = $967 - $507.50 = **$459.50/month**

**After PR (CORRECT):**
- Uses couple FBR: $1,450/month
- SSI = $1,450 - $507.50 = **$942.50/month**

**Impact: +$483/month (+$5,796/year)**

---

### Example 2: Spouse Earns $967/month (Cap Example)

**Family:**
- Woman: Healthy, earns $967/month gross
- Man: Disabled, $0 income

**Does deeming apply?**
- Woman's gross: $967 > $483 → **YES**

**Combined countable:**
- $967 - $20 - $65 = $882
- Half: $882 / 2 = $441/month

**Before PR (WRONG):**
- Individual FBR: $967
- SSI = $967 - $441 = **$526/month**

**After PR (CORRECT):**
- Couple FBR: $1,450
- Benefit before cap: $1,450 - $441 = $1,009
- **Cap at individual FBR:** min($1,009, $967) = **$967/month**

**Impact: +$441/month (+$5,292/year)**

**Note:** This demonstrates why the individual FBR cap is necessary - when gross income is just above $483, exclusions reduce countable income enough that the uncapped benefit would exceed the individual rate.

---

### Example 3: With Child Allocation

**Family:**
- Woman: Healthy, earns $3,000/month
- Man: Disabled, $0 income
- Child: Healthy, $0 income

**Child allocation:**
- $1,450 - $967 = $483/month
- Woman's gross after: $3,000 - $483 = $2,517/month

**Does deeming apply?**
- $2,517 > $483 → **YES**

**Combined countable:**
- $2,517 - $20 - $65 = $2,432
- Half: $2,432 / 2 = $1,216/month

**Before PR (WRONG):**
- Individual FBR: $967
- Benefit: $967 - $1,216 = -$849 → **$0**

**After PR (CORRECT):**
- Couple FBR: $1,450
- Benefit: $1,450 - $1,216 = **$234/month**

**Impact: +$234/month (+$2,808/year)**

---

### Example 4: No Deeming (Low Income)

**Family:**
- Woman: Healthy, earns $400/month
- Man: Disabled, $0 income

**Does deeming apply?**
- Woman's gross: $400 ≤ $483 → **NO**

**Before and After PR: SAME**
- Uses individual FBR: $967
- Man's countable: $0
- SSI = $967 - $0 = **$967/month**

**Impact: $0** (no change - this scenario was already correct)

---

## Comparison Table: Before vs. After PR

| Woman's Earned | Deeming? | Before PR (Wrong) | After PR (Correct) | Benefit Gained |
|----------------|----------|-------------------|-------------------|----------------|
| $400 | No | $967 | $967 | $0 |
| $500 | Yes | $742 | $1,225 | **+$483** |
| $967 | Yes | $526 | $967 (capped) | **+$441** |
| $1,100 | Yes | $459.50 | $942.50 | **+$483** |
| $1,500 | Yes | $242.50 | $725.50 | **+$483** |
| $2,000 | Yes | $9.50 | $492.50 | **+$483** |
| $3,000 (no child) | Yes | $0 | $0 | $0 |
| $3,000 (with child) | Yes | $0 | $234 | **+$234** |

**Key pattern:** When deeming applies, couples gain $483/month except when:
- Income is just above threshold (gain varies due to cap)
- Income is so high that even couple FBR results in $0

---

## The Fix Implementation

### 1. New Helper Variable: `is_ssi_spousal_deeming.py`
Determines when spousal deeming applies:
```python
# Check if spouse's gross income (after child allocations) > $483
spouse_deemed_income = add(person, period, [
    "ssi_earned_income_deemed_from_ineligible_spouse",
    "ssi_unearned_income_deemed_from_ineligible_spouse",
])
diff = (p.couple - p.individual) * MONTHS_IN_YEAR  # $5,796/year
return is_eligible_individual & (spouse_deemed_income > diff)
```

### 2. Fixed `ssi_amount_if_eligible.py`
```python
is_joint_claim = person("ssi_claim_is_joint", period)
deeming_applies = person("is_ssi_spousal_deeming", period)

individual_or_deeming_amount = where(
    deeming_applies,
    p.couple,  # ✅ Use couple rate when deeming!
    p.individual,
)

head_or_spouse_amount = where(
    is_joint_claim,
    p.couple / 2,
    individual_or_deeming_amount,
)
```

### 3. Added Cap in `ssi.py`
Moved cap logic from `uncapped_ssi` to `ssi` for better separation of concerns:
```python
uncapped = person("uncapped_ssi", period)

# Apply floor: cannot be negative
benefit = max_(0, uncapped)

# Apply cap when deeming: cannot exceed individual FBR
deeming_applies = person("is_ssi_spousal_deeming", period)
individual_max = p.individual * MONTHS_IN_YEAR
capped_benefit = min_(benefit, individual_max)

return where(
    deeming_applies,
    capped_benefit,
    benefit,
)
```

### 4. Refactoring Improvements

- Eliminated duplicate threshold checking by reusing `is_ssi_spousal_deeming` in `ssi_income_deemed_from_ineligible_spouse.py`
- Removed nested `where()` statements for better readability
- Better variable naming for clarity

---

## Files Modified

1. **New:** `policyengine_us/variables/gov/ssa/ssi/eligibility/income/deemed/from_ineligible_spouse/is_ssi_spousal_deeming.py`
2. **Modified:** `policyengine_us/variables/gov/ssa/ssi/ssi_amount_if_eligible.py`
3. **Modified:** `policyengine_us/variables/gov/ssa/ssi/ssi.py`
4. **Modified:** `policyengine_us/variables/gov/ssa/ssi/eligibility/income/deemed/from_ineligible_spouse/ssi_income_deemed_from_ineligible_spouse.py`
5. **Modified:** `policyengine_us/tests/policy/baseline/gov/ssa/ssi/integration_tests.yaml`

---

## Testing

All 105+ SSI tests pass with the fix, including:
- Historical CFR regulation examples (1986)
- Modern 2025 test scenarios
- Spousal deeming edge cases
- Parent-to-child deeming scenarios
- Integration tests with various family structures
- New test cases demonstrating cap behavior and child allocation impact

---

## Regulatory Compliance

This fix brings PolicyEngine into compliance with:
- **20 CFR §416.1163** - Deeming of income from an ineligible spouse
- **SSA POMS SI 01320.400** - Operational guidance for spousal deeming

The implementation now correctly follows the SSA's step-by-step deeming calculation process.

items.title: SSI Implementation Adjustments
items.body:
# SSI Implementation Adjustments Needed

## Summary
This document outlines adjustments needed to align PolicyEngine's SSI implementation with actual SSI regulations (20 CFR Part 416).

## Current Implementation vs. Legal Requirements

### 1. Spousal Deeming (20 CFR §416.1163)

#### Legal Process:
1. Calculate ineligible spouse's income
2. Deduct child allocations (from unearned first, then earned)
3. **FBR Differential Test**: If remaining ≤ (Couple FBR - Individual FBR), no deeming
4. If remaining > differential, calculate deemed amount as:
   - Combined countable income - Individual's countable income alone

#### Current Implementation:
The code in `ssi_income_deemed_from_ineligible_spouse.py` appears to follow this correctly:
- Lines 35-37: Checks if leftover > FBR differential
- Lines 45-57: Calculates deemed amount as difference between combined and individual countable

**Status**: ✅ Implementation appears correct

### 2. Parent-to-Child Deeming (20 CFR §416.1165)

#### Legal Process:
1. Calculate parents' combined income
2. Deduct allocations for ineligible children
3. Deduct parent living allowance (couple or individual FBR)
4. Apply standard SSI exclusions
5. Divide remainder equally among eligible children

#### Areas to Verify:
- Parent living allowance calculation
- Order of deductions
- Division among multiple eligible children

### 3. Child Allocations (20 CFR §416.1163(b))

#### Legal Requirement:
- Allocation per child = (Couple FBR - Individual FBR)
- Reduced by child's own income
- In 2025: $1,450 - $967 = $483/month = $5,796/year

**Status**: ✅ Correctly implemented in `ssi_ineligible_child_allocation.py`

## Test Case Discrepancies

### Case 2 from Integration Tests
- **Scenario**: One disabled adult + healthy spouse ($2,000/month) + disabled child
- **Expected per regulations**: Spouse's countable ($957.50/month) < FBR differential ($483), so no deeming
- **Actual in PolicyEngine**: Deems $11,490 (full countable amount)

**Possible Issue**: The FBR differential test may not be applying correctly in all cases.

### Case 4 from Integration Tests  
- **Scenario**: Disabled adult + healthy spouse ($3,000/month) + healthy child
- **Child allocation**: Correctly calculated as $5,796
- **Spousal deeming**: $15,102 (higher than expected)

## Recommendations

1. **Review Test Cases**: The existing test cases in `ssi_income_deemed_from_ineligible_spouse.yaml` pass, suggesting the core logic is correct. The integration test failures may indicate:
   - Different assumptions about income types (earned vs. unearned)
   - Edge cases in the calculation flow

2. **Verify Order of Operations**: Ensure that:
   - Child allocations are deducted BEFORE the FBR differential test
   - Exclusions are applied in the correct order

3. **Debug Specific Scenarios**: Run detailed traces on failing integration tests to identify where calculations diverge from expectations

## Next Steps

1. Create unit tests that exactly match the CFR examples
2. Trace through the calculation for Case 2 to identify why full amount is deemed
3. Review parent-to-child deeming implementation
4. Document any intentional policy choices that differ from strict CFR interpretation

## References
- [20 CFR §416.1163](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/20/416.1163) - Spousal Deeming
- [20 CFR §416.1165](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/20/416.1165) - Parent-to-Child Deeming
- [SSA POMS SI 01320.400](https://secure.ssa.gov/poms.nsf/lnx/0501320400) - Deeming of Income

items.title: Fix SSI Spousal Deeming: Correct Income Exclusion Order and FBR Comparison
items.body: The current SSI spousal deeming calculation incorrectly processes household income for cases with an eligible disabled individual and an ineligible working spouse. The implementation combines household incomes before applying exclusions and does not properly compare against the [Federal Benefit Rate (FBR) differential.](https://www.ssa.gov/OP_Home/cfr20/416/416-1163.htm)
